title: Design problem: proof of delivery with flaky connectivity
gist: Sam designs a driver proof-of-delivery flow that decouples a tiny 'delivered' event (with a ~20 KB thumbnail) from a resumable photo upload queue, adds glove-friendly capture, and openly flags limited maps and geospatial experience.

turns.t: Okay, let's do the design problem, we've got about, yeah, twenty minutes left, so let's give this ten or twelve. So here's the setup. You're building the delivery flow in a driver app. Driver pulls up to a stop, delivers the package, and has to capture proof of delivery, which is one or more photos, sometimes a signature. Connectivity is flaky, like, could be fine, could be nothing for an hour in a rural stretch, could be one bar in a loading dock. Dispatch wants to know as soon as possible that the stop is done. And the customer, the shipper, wants the photo, because that's how they resolve 'I never got my package' disputes. How would you approach it?
Okay. Can I ask a couple of questions first?
Please.
How many photos per stop, typically, and are they, like, required? Can a driver complete a stop without one?
Usually one, sometimes two or three for freight. Required for most customers. Some shippers make it optional.
And how many stops in a day? Ballpark.
Parcel and grocery, call it eighty to a hundred and fifty. Freight a lot fewer, maybe ten or fifteen, but bigger.
Okay, and last one, how long does the photo need to be kept on the device? Like is there a legal thing, or is it just until it's uploaded?
Let's say just until it's safely on the server.

Cool. So, I'd split it into three things that are actually pretty different. There's capture, there's the stop completion as an event, and there's the photo upload. And the main design decision is that those are decoupled. The driver should never be waiting on the network to move to the next stop.
Okay.

So capture first. Driver hits 'complete,' camera opens, they take the photo. The moment they accept it, we write it to app storage, not the camera roll, the app's own directory, and we compute a hash. We also capture metadata, the stop id, the GPS fix and its accuracy, the timestamp, both wall clock and a monotonic one in case the device clock is wrong, which, as we established, it will be. Then we compress on device. A full camera photo is like four or five megabytes, and for proof of delivery you need, what, long edge sixteen hundred pixels, JPEG at decent quality, you're around two to three hundred kilobytes. That's ten to twenty times less to upload over a bad connection, which is probably the biggest single win in this whole thing.
Do you keep the original?

I'd say no, unless the shipper needs it for some legal reason. Keeping originals is how you fill up a driver's phone by Wednesday. Which leads to the other thing, I'd check free storage at the start of the shift and warn if it's low, because you don't want to discover that at stop ninety.
That happens. That literally happens.

I believe it. Okay so then the completion. In the same local transaction as saving the photo, we write a 'stop delivered' event to the outbox. That event is tiny, it's like a few hundred bytes, it includes the photo hash and a reference, but not the photo itself. And I'd also generate a really small thumbnail, like twenty kilobytes, maybe less, and attach that to the event. So the moment there's any connection at all, even a terrible one, dispatch gets 'stop twelve delivered at 2:14, here's a tiny preview, full photo pending.' And the UI moves the driver on to the next stop immediately.
Why the thumbnail?

Two reasons. One, dispatch gets something to look at fast, which honestly covers most of the disputes, like, 'yes, it's on the porch.' And two, it's insurance. If the phone dies, or gets dropped in a canal, or the driver uninstalls the app before the full photo uploads, you at least have the thumbnail on the server. It's not great evidence, but it's a lot better than nothing.
Okay, I like that.

Then the photo upload is its own queue, separate from the event outbox, because you don't want a three hundred kilobyte upload stuck on bad signal blocking the small events behind it. That's the head-of-line thing again. I'd have the client request a presigned upload URL, and use a resumable upload, either chunked multipart or something like the tus protocol, so if you're at eighty percent and lose signal you don't start over. The server verifies the hash when it's done and then acks. And only after that ack do we delete the local file. Never before.
What about when they're on a cell connection that's technically up but awful? Like one bar.

Yeah, that's honestly a harder case than no connection. With no connection you just wait. With a bad one you can burn battery and data retrying forever. So I'd use small chunks, maybe two fifty-six kilobytes, timeouts that adapt to recent throughput, and backoff with jitter. And I'd prioritize: events first, always, then photos oldest first. And, if the shipper allows it, the depot wifi at end of shift is the backstop. So you'd show the dispatcher a stop as delivered, photo pending, and you'd expect the long tail to clear when they get back to the depot.
Can I ask about the driver side for a sec? Because the thing I think about is, the driver is holding a box, maybe wearing gloves, it's raining, there's glare. What does that screen look like to you?

Yeah, totally. So I'd want the capture to be basically one big button. The camera opens straight away when you hit complete, no extra screen in between. Big shutter button, reachable with a thumb, works with gloves, which means big targets, honestly bigger than feels right in Figma. A quick review, 'use this photo or retake,' and I'd lean on auto-accepting after a second or two unless they tap retake, because every extra tap at a hundred stops a day adds up. And the sync state should be visible but quiet. Like the stop in the list gets a little upload icon until the photo's on the server, and there's a count somewhere, 'two photos uploading.' Same lesson as before. Drivers will want to know their proof is safe, because if there's a dispute it's on them.
Yeah. That's a real thing, drivers get blamed.
Right, so it's not just a UX nicety, it's, like, their job security.

Okay, one more angle. Location. Say the shipper wants to verify the driver was actually at the address when they took the photo. And dispatch wants to see the stops on a map. How would you handle that part?

So, I'll be upfront, this is where my experience is thinner. I've done basic stuff, capturing GPS with accuracy, and I've done a simple geofence check, like is this point within some radius of the stop's coordinates, haversine distance, that kind of thing. I'd record the GPS fix and its accuracy with the photo, and I'd flag, not block, deliveries where the fix is more than, I don't know, a hundred and fifty meters from the address, because blocking is going to fail in exactly the places you don't want it to fail, like big apartment complexes or GPS bouncing around downtown between tall buildings. But the map side, rendering lots of stops, clustering, route lines, offline map tiles, I've only done that in a side project with Mapbox. I haven't done it at scale in production. I'd want to lean on whoever on the team has, and I'd learn it, but I don't want to pretend.
No, I appreciate that. It's good to know. And the flagging instead of blocking, that's the right instinct, we got burned on that exact thing.
The apartment complex thing?
The apartment complex thing. Okay, anything you'd want to add before we move on?

Just one, observability. I'd want metrics from the client on queue depth and time to upload, like p50 and p95 from capture to server ack, per region. Because otherwise you'll never know which areas are actually bad until a shipper complains.
Yep. Okay, great.

title: Sam's questions and interviewer debrief
gist: Sam asks about on-call, team size, product decisions and remote work, proposing a 1–9 p.m. Lisbon day for about 4 hours of Pacific overlap; after Sam leaves, Maya and Priya flag geospatial depth and the overlap as concerns and agree to advance Sam to the final round with Asher.

turns.t: So, your turn. What do you want to know?
Okay, I have a list, I'll try to be quick. First, on-call. What does it look like for frontend engineers?

So frontend engineers are in a rotation, but it's a separate, lighter rotation from the backend one. It's mostly the dashboard and the driver app releases. Right now it's about one week in eight. And, being honest with you, we had an outage last Thursday, the ETA service was down for about forty-seven minutes, and that was a backend issue, a Redis failover that turned into a retry storm. The frontend on-call wasn't paged into the fix, but they were in the incident channel helping with customer comms. We're also, we're working on getting the status page updated faster, that was not our best moment.
That's fair, thanks for telling me. And would on-call be in my hours, or —

We'd set it up so your on-call hours are your working hours, with a backup on Pacific time. We're not going to page you at three a.m. Lisbon time for a dashboard bug. I'll send you the on-call doc after this, it's short, it'll answer the rest.
Okay, good. Second, team size. How many people would I actually be working with?

So my org is eleven engineers right now, across routing, the ML side with Kenji, platform with Ravi, and the apps. We're hiring two senior frontend engineers, and they'd mostly sit on the driver app and the dispatcher dashboard. Day to day you'd be working with probably four or five people, plus Priya, plus Daniel, he's our staff engineer, he's kind of everywhere.
Got it. And how do product decisions get made? Like, who decides what gets built, and how much does engineering get a say?

Our head of product is Asher, you'll probably meet him in the next round. The way it works, roughly, is the quarterly priorities get set in planning, product, design, eng, sales is in there too. And within that, teams have a lot of room. Engineers write the design docs, they're in customer calls sometimes. I'll be honest, it's a sixty-person startup, so sometimes things come in sideways, a big customer wants something, a deal needs something. That's part of the job. I think engineering has a real voice, but you have to use it.
And design is pretty embedded. Like, an engineer on the driver app would be in the onboarding research sessions with me, we're redoing that whole flow right now.

That sounds great, actually. Okay, last one, and it's kind of the big one for me. Remote, and specifically time zones. I'm in Lisbon, I'm not planning to move. Most of the team is Pacific, right? What's the overlap you'd expect?

Yeah, most of us are Pacific, a few people in Seattle and one in Toronto. We're remote-first, there's no office requirement, but most of the team works roughly nine to five Pacific. What were you thinking for your hours?

So I've thought about this. I'd shift my day, work something like one p.m. to nine p.m. Lisbon. That's, right now, nine a.m. to one p.m. Pacific, so about four hours of overlap. And honestly I'm a bit of a night owl anyway, so it's not a sacrifice. And my mornings would be focus time, which you'd kind of get for free since everyone's asleep.

Four hours is workable. I won't pretend it's the same as being here. Planning would land in your evening, and there'll be days where something blows up at three p.m. Pacific and you're offline. So we'd want to be deliberate about async, like, writing things down, doing handoff notes at the end of your day, recording design reviews so you can watch them in the morning. Which honestly we should be doing anyway, so in a way it'd be good for us.
That's fair. I'd rather hear that than 'oh, time zones are no problem.'
Ha. Yeah. Anything else?
No, I think that's it. Thank you both, this was genuinely fun. The proof-of-delivery thing, I'm going to be thinking about that for a while.
Thanks Sam, really nice to meet you.
Thanks Sam. Hannah will be in touch about next steps, probably in the next couple of days. Enjoy the rest of your evening. Go to bed.
I'll try. Bye!
Okay, Sam's off. Quick gut check while it's fresh?

Strong. Like, really strong. The design story was one of the best answers I've heard to that question. Brought data, didn't bring a solution, and then admitted the designer was right about the anxiety thing. That's exactly what I want. And on the delivery flow, the gloves and glare stuff, they got there without me having to drag it out of them.

Yeah, I'm in the same place. Technically it's the strongest frontend candidate we've talked to. The sync stuff was real, like, you can't make up the wrong-year phone story. Intents instead of balances, the thumbnail as insurance, decoupling the event from the upload, that's all exactly how I'd want someone on the driver app to think. And the idempotency slip, honestly, catching it themselves was a plus, not a minus.
Totally. Concerns?

Two. Maps and geospatial. They were upfront about it, but it's thin, and a lot of the dashboard work is map-heavy, clustering, live positions, all of that. I think it's learnable, and Daniel can pair, but it's a real gap. And the time zone. Four hours of overlap is workable, but it's on the low end, and it's going to cost us something during weeks like last week.
Yeah, the time zone one is the one I'd watch. For the onboarding work we do a lot of live jam sessions. But four hours is enough if we plan for it.

Okay, so I think the recommendation is advance to the final round with Asher. I'll write that up. And I'll ask Asher to dig into the maps gap and the overlap specifically, so we're not just hand-waving it. Like, for the maps thing, maybe he walks them through the dispatcher map and asks how they'd approach clustering a few thousand live vehicles, just to see how they reason about something they haven't done. And for the overlap, a concrete scenario. It's three p.m. Pacific, the dashboard's broken for a big customer, Sam's been offline for two hours. What does the handoff look like.
Agreed. I'll get my scorecard in tonight.
Mine'll be in by tomorrow morning. I'll ping Hannah to get the final scheduled, ideally next week. We don't want to lose this one.
No, we really don't. Okay, bye.
Bye.
